entries.title: He Asked About Her. Did They Meet?

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: In this simplified look at Persuasion chapter thirteen, Anne learns that Captain Wentworth asked about her. Which conclusion follows? First: They met at Kellynch. Second: He wanted information about her. Listen for the difference between asking about someone and speaking to them.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: The second conclusion fits. Asking about Anne doesn't establish that they met. This chapter gives Anne news about him, not a reunion with him. A small detail can matter emotionally without telling us everything a character feels.

entries.prompt: Does asked about her prove that he spoke to her?
entries.answer: No. It describes an enquiry about her, not a conversation with her.

entries.title: Costumes Optional Means You Have a Choice
entries.hook: Do you have to dress up?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: The invitation says costumes optional. I haven't got one. Should I say I can't come?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Optional means you can choose. You can ask: Are casual clothes okay? You don't need to turn a clothing question into a cancellation.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: The host says casual clothes are fine. Then I'll reply: Great, I'll come in casual clothes. Thanks for checking.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Now you've answered the invitation and checked the one detail you needed. You haven't promised to buy anything or invent an excuse.

entries.prompt: Does optional mean required, or your choice?
entries.answer: Your choice. Ask about the detail if the invitation is unclear.

entries.title: Anne Turns Worry into Practical Help
entries.hook: Comfort can become a practical plan.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Here is a simplified retelling of one moment in Persuasion chapter thirteen. The Musgroves are worried about Louisa. They also dread Anne leaving. Anne cannot remove their worry with a cheerful promise, but she sees something useful they can do.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: She encourages them to go to Lyme and helps with their preparations. Being nearer Louisa also gives them a way to relieve some of the Harvilles' responsibilities. Anne's help is practical, not a claim that everything is suddenly fine.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Notice the move from feeling helpless to finding a useful action. In everyday English, you might ask: What would actually help right now? That sentence is our modern practice, not a quotation from Austen.

entries.prompt: Does Anne erase their worry, or help them act on it?
entries.answer: She helps them act. Useful support need not promise an outcome nobody knows.

entries.title: Ask Before Bringing an Extra Guest
entries.hook: An invitation isn't a guest list.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Our fictional party host invited me. My friend wants to come too, so I'll just arrive with them. One more person won't matter, will it?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: It might matter to the host. Ask first: Would it be okay if I brought a friend? That's a question, not an announcement that you've already decided.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: The host says the room is full. I'll say: No problem. I'll come on my own. I haven't promised my friend a place.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Exactly. Your reply accepts the actual invitation. You don't have to argue, guess the host's reasons, or share anyone's personal details to practise the question.

entries.prompt: Should you ask before promising your friend they can come?
entries.answer: Yes. A clear question leaves the host free to answer honestly.
